key_terms.meaning: A service or capability the system must provide, e.g. 'the app shall transfer money to a saved payee'
A quality or constraint on how well the system works, e.g. 'a transfer shall confirm within 3 seconds'
A statement in the customer's language of what users need, written for understanding, not for design
A detailed, precise, testable restatement of a user requirement for the developers
A short early check of technical, economic, legal, operational and schedule viability before full analysis
The loop of feasibility, elicitation, analysis, specification, validation and management
Any person or group affected by the system: user, customer, sponsor, maintainer, regulator, support staff
Planned group sessions where users, developers and customers jointly list needs, constraints and priorities
Checking that the written requirements are complete, consistent, correct and testable
Keeping every requirement identified, versioned, traceable and under change control through the project
A recorded link from a requirement to its source, its design element, its code and its test cases
The agreed document stating what the system must do, for whom, under what constraints, and how it will be judged
A role outside the system (person, device or other system) that interacts with it to reach a goal
A named goal-driven interaction between actors and the system, with a main flow and alternate flows
One concrete path through a use case, usually written as numbered steps of an instance
A diagram of the problem's classes, their attributes and operations, and the relationships between them
A model of the states one object can be in, the events that move it, and the actions it performs
A diagram of external entities, processes, data stores and data flows, showing transformation of data and no control or timing
A method that maps customer needs to ranked technical responses so design effort follows customer value
The matrix built in QFD: customer needs (whats) down the side, technical responses (hows) across the top, scored relationships between them

takeaways: Separate what the system does (functional) from how well or under what limits it does it (non-functional); testability belongs to both.
Requirements engineering is a loop, not a form: the same requirements are elicited, analysed, written, validated and then changed under control.
A feasibility study is cheap insurance; it can end a project before large money is spent.
Elicitation means talking to every affected group, because one manager's view never covers the whole problem.
Validation asks 'did we write the right requirements?'; verification asks 'did we build the thing right?'.
An SRS is useful only when each requirement can be tested, so write numbers with units, not adjectives.
Use cases organise requirements around user goals; scenarios and state models fill in the paths and the order of events.
A DFD shows data moving and being transformed; a class model shows things and their relationships; keep the two views consistent.
bank_note: Long answers here are usually marked on classification plus a worked diagram or example: distinguish requirement types, walk the requirements engineering process, draw and level a DFD or use case model, build a house of quality, and justify validation and change-control choices.

bank.q: Classify software requirements. Distinguish functional from non-functional requirements and give four examples of each for an online railway reservation system.
outline: Definition of a requirement as capability or condition
Functional: capability or service the system must provide
Non-functional: quality attribute or constraint on the system as a whole
Sub-types of non-functional: product, organisational, external; performance, security, usability, reliability
Four functional and four non-functional examples for the reservation system with measurable values
Why the separation matters: different tests, different design decisions

bank.q: Explain the requirements engineering process and the role of the feasibility study in it.
outline: Process as a loop: feasibility, elicitation, analysis, specification, validation, management
Inputs and outputs of each stage
Feasibility types: technical, economic, legal, operational, schedule
Cost-benefit and rough estimate at feasibility stage
Why the process repeats: new stakeholders, change requests, feedback from validation
Where requirements management sits across the whole loop

bank.q: What is a software requirements specification? Describe its standard structure and the characteristics of a good SRS.
outline: Definition of SRS as the agreed statement of what, for whom, under what constraints
Typical sections: purpose, scope, definitions, overall description, specific requirements, interfaces, constraints, acceptance criteria
User requirements versus system requirements inside the document
Good SRS properties: correct, unambiguous, complete, consistent, ranked, verifiable, modifiable, traceable
Interface specification: user, hardware, software, communication
Mention of a standards reference for SRS content without inventing clause numbers

bank.q: Explain data flow diagrams: symbols, rules of levelling and balancing, with a small example.
outline: Four symbols: external entity, process, data store, data flow
What a DFD deliberately does not show: control, timing, decisions
Context (level-0) diagram with one process
Level-1 decomposition and numbering scheme
Levelling rule: child diagram inputs and outputs must match the parent process
Balancing, no black holes or miracles, unique names, no direct entity-to-entity flow

bank.q: Apply quality function deployment to a UPI payment app. Build a house of quality with at least five customer needs and four technical responses, and rank the responses.
outline: Customer needs (whats): fast transfer, low failure, simple screen, refund speed, privacy
Importance rating for each need, totalling 1 or 100
Technical responses (hows): transaction timeout budget, retry logic, UI steps, refund automation, encryption
Relationship matrix scored 9/3/1 or 9/3/0 with blanks for none
Compute absolute weight per response as sum of importance times relationship score
Rank, note roof trade-offs such as security versus speed
Conclusion on which response gets engineering effort first

bank.q: For the tatkal booking flow of a train reservation system, identify actors, draw a use case diagram and write one fully described use case with a main flow and two alternate flows.
outline: Actors: passenger, payment gateway, railway database, admin; primary versus secondary
Use case diagram: system boundary, actors, use cases, associations
Include and extend used correctly, generalisation where useful
Use case description template: name, actors, preconditions, main flow, alternate flows, postconditions
Alternate flows such as payment failure and seat sold out
One scenario written as a concrete instance of the main flow

bank.q: Draw a context diagram and a level-1 data flow diagram for a college library system, and explain how you keep the two balanced.
outline: External entities: student, librarian, supplier, accounts
Context diagram: single process, all flows to and from entities
Level-1 processes: issue book, return book, search catalogue, acquire book, fine handling
Data stores: book master, member master, loan register, fine ledger
Numbering of processes and matching of net inputs and outputs with the parent
Checklist for correctness: no entity-to-entity flow, no data store-to-store flow, no unnamed flows

bank.q: Model an ATM cash withdrawal with a class diagram, a sequence diagram and a state diagram. Explain what each model adds.
outline: Classes: Card, Account, Transaction, ATM, Bank; attributes and operations
Associations and multiplicities, e.g. one account to many transactions
Sequence diagram: actor, boundary, control and entity objects with ordered messages
State diagram for the ATM or the transaction: idle, card inserted, PIN entered, dispensing, completed, error
Events and guards on transitions, entry and exit actions
Statement of what each view contributes: structure, message order, lifecycle

bank.q: A draft requirements document for a hospital appointment system is given to you. Describe how you would validate it using checklists, inspections, prototyping and test-case generation.
outline: Purpose of validation: right requirements, not right code
Checklist review against standard SRS properties
Formal inspection: roles, preparation, meeting, defect log, follow-up
Prototype of the booking screen to check understanding with doctors and receptionists
Derive at least one acceptance test per requirement to expose untestable wording
Record defects, agree changes, revalidate the baseline

bank.q: Read this requirement: 'The system should be fast, user friendly and handle many users.' Analyse its defects and rewrite it as verifiable functional and non-functional requirements with units.
outline: Defects: vague adjectives, no actors, no conditions, no measurement, not testable
Separate the functional intent from the quality intent
Rewrite with measurable thresholds and units, e.g. response time in seconds at a stated load
State the load and concurrency assumption explicitly
State the measurement method so the test is repeatable
Rules for verifiable wording: no comparatives without a baseline

bank.q: Requirements errors are the costliest to fix late. Discuss, and evaluate how baseline, change control and traceability reduce that cost.
outline: Why late discovery is expensive: rework spreads to design, code, tests, documentation
Typical sources of requirements error: missing stakeholders, ambiguity, assumed knowledge
Baseline: an agreed, versioned set of requirements as the reference for change
Change control: request, impact analysis, decision, update, notification
Traceability forwards and backwards to design, code and tests
Impact on effort estimation and on regression testing
Reasonable conclusion on cost of control versus cost of rework

bank.q: Compare structured analysis with data flow diagrams and object-oriented analysis with use case and class models for a food delivery application. Which do you recommend and why?
outline: DFD view: processes, data stores, flows; strong for data transformation and for communicating with users
DFD weaknesses: no control, no timing, processes and data kept separate, poor mapping to objects
Object view: actors, use cases, classes, responsibilities, states; strong for evolving and interactive systems
Mapping between the two views and the need for consistency
Criteria: complexity of data transformation, expected change, team skill, need for concurrency and state
Justified recommendation with the residual role of the other model

bank.q: A hospital appointment system has many conflicting stakeholders: doctors, nurses, receptionists, patients, billing and a regulator. Evaluate how you would combine collaborative gathering, use case modelling and QFD to reach an agreed, ranked requirement set.
outline: Stakeholder identification and viewpoint analysis to expose conflicts
Collaborative session: agenda, facilitator, neutral recording, rules for the group
Use cases to bind each viewpoint to concrete goals and to reveal missing actors
QFD to convert needs into ranked technical responses and to make trade-offs explicit
Handling conflict: negotiation, priority ranking, cost and schedule trade-off, escalation path
Regulatory constraints treated as non-negotiable non-functional requirements
Validation and baseline at the end, with traceability to acceptance tests

bank.q: 'Requirements are never stable, so heavy requirements work is wasted.' Evaluate this statement for a plan-driven project and for an agile project.
outline: Why requirements change: market, regulation, better understanding, technology
Cost of change rises with project stage, so early clarity still pays
Plan-driven: full specification, baseline, formal change control, traceability
Agile: lightweight requirement statements, short feedback cycles, change welcomed
Common ground: elicitation, validation and traceability are needed in both
Risk-based judgement on how much specification a project needs
Balanced conclusion, not one-sided

glossary.def: A capability the software must provide or a condition it must satisfy.
A statement of a service, input-output behaviour or function the system must perform.
A statement about quality, performance or constraint that applies to the system as a whole.
A natural-language statement of what users need, written for customers to read and agree.
A structured, precise and testable version of a user requirement written for developers.
A requirement that comes from the rules and conventions of the application domain, not from a single user.
A short assessment of whether a proposed system is worth building and can be built within limits.
The activity of drawing out requirements from stakeholders and from documents and existing systems.
Anyone who affects or is affected by the system, including indirect users and maintainers.
One stakeholder's angle on the system, used to organise and cross-check requirements.
Classifying, modelling and negotiating requirements to remove conflict, overlap and gaps.
Agreeing which competing requirements will be met, ranked and possibly deferred.
Confirming that the written requirements are the right ones and are checkable.
A formal, role-based team review of a document against a checklist, with a logged defect list.
Controlling requirement identity, versions, change and links throughout the project.
A formally agreed and versioned set of items that later changes must be measured against.
A table linking each requirement to its source, design element, code and test cases.
The software requirements specification, the agreed document defining what the system must do and how it will be judged.
A goal-driven interaction between external actors and the system, described by a main flow and alternates.
A role played by a person, device or system that interacts with the system from outside its boundary.
One specific path through a use case, written with concrete values or as a narrative.
A structural model of classes, attributes, operations, associations and multiplicities.
A behavioural model showing objects and the time-ordered messages they exchange.
A behavioural model of states, events, guards and actions for a single object or the whole system.
A model of external entities, processes, data stores and data flows, with no control or timing shown.
Decomposing a DFD process into a child diagram whose flows match the parent's flows.
A structured method mapping customer needs to ranked technical responses.
The QFD matrix of customer needs, technical responses and their scored relationships.
